title: Job Sequencing With Deadlines
statement:
You are given `n` jobs. Job `i` has a **deadline** `deadline[i]` and a **profit** `profit[i]`. Every job takes exactly **one unit of time** and only one job can run at a time. Time starts at 0, so the unit slots are `1, 2, 3, ...`: a job that runs in slot `t` finishes at time `t`, and it earns its profit only if `t ≤ deadline[i]`.

You may skip any job. Choose a subset of the jobs and an order for them so that every chosen job meets its deadline and the total profit is **maximized**.

Print two integers: the number of jobs in an optimal schedule and the maximum total profit. (All profits are positive, so every maximum-profit schedule contains the same number of jobs and the output is unique.)
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
Each of the next `n` lines contains two integers `deadline[i]` and `profit[i]`.
outputFormat: Print two space-separated integers: the number of scheduled jobs and the maximum total profit.

examples.explanation: Slot 1 can only be used by a job with deadline at least 1, slot 2 by deadline at least 2, and so on. Take the job with profit 40 (slot 1), 30 (slot 2) and 20 (slot 3). The jobs with profit 25 and 10 have deadlines 2 and 1, but slots 1 and 2 are already taken, and the job with profit 5 would need slot 3 as well. Total 40 + 30 + 20 = 90.
All deadlines are far away, so every job fits in one of the first four slots and the total is 7 + 9 + 4 + 8 = 28.
Every job must run in slot 1, so only one of them can be chosen; take the most profitable.

hints: A set of jobs is feasible exactly when, after sorting by deadline, the k-th job has deadline at least k.
Process jobs in increasing deadline order and keep the profits of the jobs you have accepted so far in a min-heap.
If the heap ever holds more jobs than the current deadline allows, drop the smallest profit. Deadlines up to 10^9 never matter beyond n.
